'''''Battlestar Galactica''''' is an American [[military science fiction]] television series, and part of the [[Battlestar Galactica|''Battlestar Galactica'' franchise]]. The show was developed by [[Ronald D. Moore]] and executive produced by Moore and [[David Eick]] as a "re-imagining"<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2006/01/23/across-the-universe|title=Across the Universe|first=Nancy|last=Franklin|date=January 23, 2006|magazine=The New Yorker|access-date=January 29, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070816111900/http://www.newyorker.com/archive/2006/01/23/060123crte_television|archive-date=August 16, 2007|url-status=live}}</ref> of the 1978 ''[[Battlestar Galactica (1978 TV series)|Battlestar Galactica]]'' television series created by [[Glen A. Larson]]. The pilot for the series first aired as a [[Battlestar Galactica (TV miniseries)|three-hour miniseries]] in December 2003 on the [[Syfy|Sci-Fi Channel]], which was then followed by four regular seasons, ending its run on March 20, 2009. The cast includes [[Edward James Olmos]], [[Mary McDonnell]], [[Katee Sackhoff]], [[Jamie Bamber]], [[James Callis]], [[Tricia Helfer]], and [[Grace Park (actress)|Grace Park]].

''Battlestar Galactica'' is set in a distant star system, where a civilization of humans live on a group of planets known as the [[Twelve Colonies of Kobol]]. In the past, the Colonies had been at war with an android race of their own creation, known as the [[Cylon (Battlestar Galactica)|Cylons]]. With the unwitting help of a human scientist named [[Gaius Baltar]] (Callis), the Cylons launch a sudden [[sneak attack]] on the Colonies, laying waste to the planets and devastating their populations. Out of a population of several billion, there are about 50,000 human survivors; most were aboard civilian space ships that were not near the initial attacks. Of all the Colonial Fleet, the [[Battlestar Galactica (ship)|Battlestar ''Galactica'']] (an older ship about to be decommissioned and turned into a museum) appears to be the only military capital ship that survived the attack. Under the leadership of Colonial Fleet officer Commander [[William Adama|William "Bill" Adama]] (Olmos) and President [[Laura Roslin]] (McDonnell), the ''Galactica'' and its crew take up the task of leading the small fleet of refugee survivors into space in search of a fabled thirteenth colony known as [[Earth in science fiction|Earth]].

The series received critical acclaim at the time and since, including a [[Peabody Award]], the [[Television Critics Association]]'s Program of the Year Award, a placement inside ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]''{{'}}s 100 Best TV Shows of All-Time and 19 Emmy nominations for its writing, directing, costume design, visual effects, sound mixing and sound editing, with three Emmy wins (visual effects and sound editing).<ref name="top100">{{cite news |last=Poniewozik |first=James |url=http://entertainment.time.com/2007/09/06/the-100-best-tv-shows-of-all-time/slide/battlestar-galactica-2/ |magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]] |title=The 100 Best TV Shows of All-Time |access-date=December 8, 2008 |date=September 6, 2007 |archive-date=October 22, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111022125613/http://entertainment.time.com/2007/09/06/the-100-best-tv-shows-of-all-time/slide/battlestar-galactica-2/ |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.emmys.com/shows/battlestar-galactica |title=Battlestar Galactica |website=Emmys.com |access-date=May 20, 2018 |archive-date=May 20, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180520194825/https://www.emmys.com/shows/battlestar-galactica |url-status=live }}</ref> In 2019, ''[[The New York Times]]'' placed the show on its list of "The 20 Best TV Dramas Since ''[[The Sopranos]]''", a period many critics call a "[[Golden Age of Television (2000s–present)|golden age of television]]".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2019/arts/television/best-drama-series.html |title=The 20 Best TV Dramas Since 'The Sopranos' |work=The New York Times |date=January 10, 2019 |access-date=March 27, 2019 |archive-date=April 12, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190412155500/https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2019/arts/television/best-drama-series.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

The series was followed by the prequel [[spin-off (media)|spin-off]] TV series ''[[Caprica]]'', which aired for one season in 2010. A further spin-off, ''[[Battlestar Galactica: Blood & Chrome]]'', was released in November 2012 as a [[web series]] of ten 10-minute episodes and aired on February 10, 2013, on [[Syfy]] as a televised movie.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/live-feed/battlestar-galactica-blood-chrome-premiere-386601 |title='Battlestar Galactica: Blood & Chrome' to Premiere Online Before Debuting on TV |first=Philiana |last=Ng |work=The Hollywood Reporter |date=November 5, 2012 |access-date=December 31, 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.thefutoncritic.com/news/2012/12/26/exclusive-battlestar-galactica-blood-and-chrome-to-make-tv-premiere-sunday-february-10-on-syfy-726420/10128/ |title=Exclusive: "Battlestar Galactica: Blood & Chrome" to Make TV Premiere Sunday, February 10 on Syfy |publisher=The Futon Critic |date=December 26, 2012 |access-date=December 31, 2012 }}</ref>

== Series overview ==
{{Main|List of Battlestar Galactica (2004 TV series) episodes}}
{{:List of Battlestar Galactica (2004 TV series) episodes}}

''Battlestar Galactica'' continued from the 2003 miniseries to chronicle the journey of the last surviving humans from the [[Twelve Colonies of Kobol]], after their nuclear annihilation by the [[Cylon (re-imagining)|Cylons]]. The survivors are led by President [[Laura Roslin]] and Commander [[William Adama]] in a ragtag fleet of ships with the [[Battlestar Galactica (ship)|Battlestar ''Galactica'']], an old but powerful warship, as its command ship. Pursued by Cylons intent on wiping out the remnants of the human race, the survivors travel across the galaxy looking for the fabled and long-lost "thirteenth" colony: [[Earth (Battlestar Galactica)|Earth]]. Unlike most [[space opera]] series, ''Battlestar Galactica'' has no [[Extraterrestrial life|humanoid aliens]] (the antagonists are man-made Cylon androids), the primary armaments used by both military forces utilize bullets, [[Railgun|rail guns]], and missiles instead of lasers, and the series intentionally avoids [[technobabble]].<ref name=nym080403>{{cite news |author=Everett Bogue |url=https://www.vulture.com/2008/04/how_to_convince_your_girlfrien.html |title=How to Convince Your Girlfriend (or Boyfriend) That 'Battlestar' Is Not 'Star Trek' |date=April 3, 2008 |work=[[New York (magazine)|New York]] |access-date=December 3, 2021 |archive-date=January 25, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090125014234/http://nymag.com/daily/entertainment/2008/04/how_to_convince_your_girlfrien.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Instead, most of the stories deal with the apocalyptic fallout of the destruction of the Twelve Colonies upon the survivors, and the moral choices they must make as they deal with the decline of the human race and their war with the Cylons. Stories also portray the concept of perpetuated cycles of hate and violence driving the human-Cylon conflict, and religion, with the implication of a "God" whose possibly angelic agents appear to certain main characters (most notably [[Gaius Baltar]]).

Over the course of the show's four seasons, the war between the Colonials and the Cylons takes many twists and turns. Despite the animosity on both sides, the humans and a faction of the Cylons eventually form an uneasy alliance, in the wake of the Cylon Civil War. The Cylon leader, a [[List of Battlestar Galactica (2004 TV series) characters|Cylon-humanoid]] "Number One" named [[John Cavil]], precipitated the schism in the Cylon ranks. Cavil deceives the other models by obsessively hiding the identities and origins of the remaining five humanoid Cylon models, the "Final Five", who, known only to him, are a more ancient type of Cylon, created by a previous iteration of human civilization. Other plotlines involve the mysterious destiny of [[Kara Thrace|Kara "Starbuck" Thrace]], who is the subject of a prophecy claiming that she is the "Harbinger of Death" who will "lead them all [humanity] to its end", as well as the redemption of Gaius Baltar through the Cylons' monotheistic religion, after he becomes a pariah within the fleet.

In the final episodes, an inexplicably resurrected Kara Thrace leads the surviving humans and their Cylon allies to a new planet, which Adama names "Earth". The first group of survivors settle in ancient Africa.  The "real" Earth that the Colonials had searched for during their years in space was revealed in an earlier episode to have been originally inhabited thousands of years before by a previous form of humanoid Cylons; the "Final Five" were the last of these Cylons. Ironically, these humanoid Cylons had created their own Centurion robotic slaves, who waged a nuclear attack against their masters, devastating the planet and making it uninhabitable. The new Earth is found to be inhabited by early humans, who are genetically compatible with the humans from ''Galactica'' and the rest of the fleet, but who possess only the most rudimentary civilization.

The surviving humans and humanoid Cylons settle on the new planet Earth; they discard all [[technology]], destroying the fleet by flying it into the [[Sun]], in an attempt to break the human-Cylon cycle of conflict and begin anew with the tribal humans already present on the new Earth. The surviving Cylon Centurions are given possession of the remaining Cylon Basestar, and proceed to jump away from Earth. In the final scenes, modern-day Earth humans are shown to be descendants of the colonists, their humanoid Cylon allies, and the early humans.

At the end of the series finale, an angelic Baltar and Cylon Number Six are walking along a sidewalk in modern-day [[New York City]]. They are unseen and unheard by the people around them. As the two walk, they notice technologically advanced robots, computers, and other cybernetic devices, and they talk about the technological advancements the humans have made since the Colonials and Humanoid Cylons first arrived on this Earth, over 150,000 years earlier. Cylon Number Six and Baltar have an exchange over one of the ongoing themes from the series: "All of this has happened before. But the question remains, does all of this have to happen again?" Consequently, the revelation that ''Battlestar Galactica'' takes place in our collective [[prehistoric]] past means that unlike most [[space opera]] science fiction stories, the series is a [[Alternate history|fictional]] tale of [[ancient history]] rather than [[future history]], and serves as a fictional tale of origin for modern humanity.

== Themes and allusions ==
''Time'' described ''Battlestar Galactica'' as "a gripping sci-fi allegory of the [[war on terror]], complete with monotheistic [[fundamentalism|religious fundamentalists]] (here genocidal cyborgs called Cylons), [[sleeper cell]]s, civil-liberties crackdowns and even a prisoner-[[torture]] scandal".<ref name="time">{{cite news |url=http://content.time.com/time/arts/article/0,8599,1141640,00.html |title=Best of 2005: Television |last=Poniewozik |first=James |magazine=Time |date=December 16, 2005 |access-date=December 3, 2021 |archive-date=May 27, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080527042310/http://www.time.com/time/arts/article/0%2C8599%2C1141640%2C00.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> The show attempted to maintain its realism by referring to familiar elements of contemporary history – [[Laura Roslin]]'s swearing in on Colonial One directly "cited the swearing in of [[Lyndon B. Johnson]] after the Kennedy assassination"<ref name="space_balls">{{cite web |url=http://www.salon.com/entertainment/tv/review/2006/11/10/battlestar/index.html |title=Space Balls |author=Miller, Laura |work=Salon |date=November 10, 2006 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110215104951/http://www.salon.com/entertainment/tv/review/2006/11/10/battlestar/index.html |archive-date=February 15, 2011 }}</ref> – and the developing political situation since the [[September 11, 2001 attacks]]. Many people have drawn parallels between the Cylons and [[Al Qaeda]]"<ref name="intergalactic_terror">{{cite magazine |url=https://www.rollingstone.com/news/story/9183391/intergalactic_terror |title=Intergalactic Terror |author=Gavin Edwards |magazine=[[Rolling Stone]] |date=January 27, 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090208135051/http://www.rollingstone.com/news/story/9183391/intergalactic_terror |archive-date=February 8, 2009 |url-status=dead |quote=In its second season, this remake of the 1978 camp classic has become -- no joke -- TV's most vivid depiction of the post-9/11 world and what happens to a society at war. }}</ref> and according to ''[[The Guardian]]'' "''Battlestar Galactica'' is the only award-winning drama that dares tackle the war on terror".<ref name="final_frontier">{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/media/2007/jan/13/tvandradio.broadcasting |title=The final frontier |author=Martin, Dan |work=The Guardian |date=January 13, 2007 |location=London |access-date=December 14, 2016 |archive-date=March 14, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160314222748/http://www.theguardian.com/media/2007/jan/13/tvandradio.broadcasting |url-status=live }}</ref> The show has also tackled issues regarding [[clandestine cell system|terrorist sleeper cells]] with stories involving the reality and fear of Cylon [[suicide attack]]s, Cylon Number 5 (Aaron Doral) in the episode called "Litmus," sneaks aboard ''Galactica'' and blows himself up in the middle of the corridor and [[sleeper agent]] Lt. Sharon "Boomer" Valerii activates after destroying a Cylon basestar and shooting Commander Adama at the end of season 1. (Note that Sharon, as with some of the other human-form Cylons, had no idea that she was a Cylon.) Similar themes are revisited in season 3 (Episode 3.1, "Occupation") with a far different perspective: the humans, rather than the Cylons, are the suicide bombers. It has been suggested that these plotlines extensively "hinted at war-on-terrorism overtones."<ref name="battlestar_iraqtica">{{cite web |url=http://www.slate.com/id/2151425/ |title=Battlestar: Iraqtica. Does the hit television show support the Iraqi insurgency |author=Ackerman, Spencer |work=Slate |date=October 13, 2006 |access-date=May 6, 2009 |archive-date=July 14, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090714232847/http://www.slate.com/id/2151425 |url-status=live }}</ref> After 9/11, the original series' "broad premise – the human military's struggles in the wake of a massive terrorist attack – suddenly gained resonance"<ref name="final_frontier" /> and let the show tackle issues like suicide bombings, torture ("evoking the darker side of the war on terror"<ref name="battlestar_iraqtica" />) and "civil liberties crackdowns".<ref name="final_frontier" />

Executive producer Ronald D. Moore points out that the Cylons and Al Qaeda are not necessarily intended to be allegorical: "They have aspects of Al Qaeda and they have aspects of the [[Catholic Church]] and they have aspects of America."<ref name="intergalactic_terror" /> On the other hand, abortion is illegal throughout the fleet, because the survival of what remains of humanity is at stake. In contrast, with the New Caprica storyline the show's humans have been discussed as an allegory not for an America under attack but for an occupied people mounting an [[insurgency]] and turning to suicide bombings as a tactic. There is a consensus that with "its third season, the show has morphed into a stinging allegorical critique of [[History of Iraq#Recent history (2003–present)|America's three-year occupation of Iraq]]"<ref name="battlestar_galacticons">{{cite web |url=http://prospect.org/cs/articles?articleId=12172 |title=Battlestar Galacticons |author=Reed, Brad |work=The American Prospect |date=October 27, 2006 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111001165107/http://prospect.org/cs/articles?articleId=12172 |archive-date=October 1, 2011 }}</ref> as the "cameras record Cylon occupation raids on unsuspecting human civilians with the [[Night vision|night-vision]] green familiar to any TV news viewer. The reasoning of the Cylons is horrifically familiar, they would prefer not to be brutal but they won't accept the failure of a glorious mission."<ref name="battlestar_iraqtica" /> According to ''[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]]'' "If this sounds like Iraq, it should",<ref name="battlestar_iraqtica" /> and "In unmistakable terms, ''Battlestar Galactica'' is telling viewers that insurgency (like, say, the one in Iraq) might have some moral flaws, such as the whole suicide bombing thing, but is ultimately virtuous and worthy of support."<ref name="battlestar_iraqtica" /> The "really audacious stroke of this season was showing us a story about a suicide bomber from the point of view of the bomber and his comrades... because the cause of this terrorist was unquestioningly our own. We sympathize with the insurgents wholeheartedly."<ref name="space_balls" /> If the Cylon occupying force is an allegory of the Coalition Forces in Iraq, then some of the other references are equally controversial; the "scene of the shiny, terrifying Cylon centurions (a servant class of robots that actually look like robots) marching down the main road of New Caprica while the devastated colonists looked on was the [[Battle of France|Nazis marching into Paris]]."<ref name="space_balls" />

Although [[David Eick]] has said the production staff "don't need to say 'OK, let's do the episode where we're gonna do the [[Abu Ghraib torture and prisoner abuse|Abu Ghraib scandal]]'" and points out that events depicted on New Caprica "are as much a story rooted in political tales like the [[Vichy France]] or [[Vietnam War|Vietnam]]" as current events, he acknowledges that they "do gravitate in those directions when it comes to the storytelling".<ref name="final_frontier" />

== Music ==
{{Main|Music of Battlestar Galactica (2004 TV series)}}

The opening theme is a [[New-age music|new-age]]-inflected version of the [[Gayatri Mantra]], a [[Hinduism|Hindu]] hymn dedicated to the solar deity [[Savitr]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.syfy.co.uk/blogs/battlestar-galactica-end-season-review-part-2 |title=Battlestar Galactica End of Season Review - Part 2 |publisher=Syfy.co.uk |first=Charlie |last=Benjamin |access-date=August 2, 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140606231923/http://www.syfy.co.uk/blogs/battlestar-galactica-end-season-review-part-2 |archive-date=June 6, 2014 }}</ref>

[[Bear McCreary]] was the primary composer for the television series, having assisted [[Richard Gibbs]] on the [[Battlestar Galactica (TV miniseries)|3-hour miniseries]]. When the show was picked up, Gibbs opted not to devote full-time to the regular series' production and McCreary became the composer.  He scored over 70 episodes.  Six ''Battlestar Galactica'' soundtrack albums have been released to great critical acclaim - one for the miniseries, one for each of the four seasons, and one combining music from the inter-season ''[[Battlestar Galactica: Razor|Razor]]'' and post-finale prequel ''[[Battlestar Galactica: The Plan|The Plan]]''. The ''[[Chicago Tribune]]'s'' Maureen Ryan hailed the music as "sensational" and "innovative",<ref name="ct080616">{{cite news |author=Ryan, Maureen |url=http://featuresblogs.chicagotribune.com/entertainment_tv/2008/06/battlestar-ga-1.html |title='Battlestar Galactica' provides some Earth-shattering 'Revelations' |date=June 16, 2008 |work=[[Chicago Tribune]] |access-date=March 18, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090329055809/http://featuresblogs.chicagotribune.com/entertainment_tv/2008/06/battlestar-ga-1.html |archive-date=March 29, 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref> Joanna Weiss of ''[[The Boston Globe]]'' praised McCreary as a "visionary composer" who did much to create "the rich atmosphere of ''Battlestar''",<ref name="jweiss">{{cite news |author=Weiss, Joanna |url=https://archive.boston.com/ae/tv/articles/2009/04/21/battlestar_prequel_brings_back_the_doom/ |title='Battlestar' prequel brings back the doom |date=April 21, 2009 |work=[[The Boston Globe]] |access-date=December 3, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090423225610/http://www.boston.com/ae/tv/articles/2009/04/21/battlestar_prequel_brings_back_the_doom/ |archive-date=April 23, 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref> Alan Sepinwall, then of ''[[The Star-Ledger]]'' described McCreary's work on the show as "transcendent"<ref name="sep080622">{{cite news |author=Sepinwall, Alan |url=https://www.nj.com/entertainment/tv/2008/06/sepinwall_on_tv_michael_giacch.html |title=Sepinwall on TV: Michael Giacchino and Bear McCreary, score keepers |date=June 22, 2008 |work=[[The Star-Ledger]] |access-date=March 18, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090321130959/http://www.nj.com/entertainment/tv/index.ssf/2008/06/sepinwall_on_tv_michael_giacch.html |archive-date=March 21, 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref> and ''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]'' said "''Galactica'' offers some of the most innovative music on TV today."<ref name="jburl">{{cite news |url=https://variety.com/2008/scene/awards/battlestar-galactica-music-takes-off-1117986684/ |title='Battlestar Galactica' music takes off |last=Burlingame |first=Jon |date=March 30, 2008 |work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] |access-date=July 18, 2009 |archive-date=March 4, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304222121/http://variety.com/2008/scene/awards/battlestar-galactica-music-takes-off-1117986684/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

The music of ''Battlestar Galactica'' displays a wide variety of influences and intentionally tries to avoid the "usual" style of a science fiction score. For some of the series' more important episodes, McCreary was granted a full orchestra. Character themes and [[leitmotif]]s gradually took on importance, despite being avoided earlier. A variety of instruments have been used. One season 4 episode employed: [[dizi (instrument)|Chinese membrane flute]], [[Bansuri|Indian bansuri flute]], [[duduk]] (Armenian woodwind), [[erhu]] (Chinese violin), [[yaylı tambur]] (a Turkish lute), [[Goblet drum|dumbek]] (Middle Eastern drum), Japanese taiko drums and four brass players, 30 string players and a 12-voice choir.<ref name="jburl"/>

There have been several live concerts featuring the music of ''Battlestar Galactica''. In April 2008, more than 1,000 fans attended two sold-out shows at L.A.'s Roxy on Sunset Boulevard, with some fans flying in from as far as England and Australia.<ref name="jburl"/> A ballet based on McCreary's scores for ''Galactica'' premiered on March 7, 2009, for a 13-week run. Entitled "Prelude to War", it was performed by the dancers of the Theaterhagen in [[Hagen]], Germany with choreography by Ricardo Fernando, and the Hagen Philharmonic Orchestra conducted by Bernhard Steiner.<ref name="ballet">{{cite news |author=McCreary, Bear |url=http://www.bearmccreary.com/blog/?p=1700 |title="Prelude to War" Ballet Premiere in Germany |date=March 12, 2009 |work=BearMcCreary.com |access-date=July 18, 2009 |archive-date=May 31, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090531222842/http://www.bearmccreary.com/blog/?p=1700 |url-status=live }}</ref>

== Broadcast and release ==
The first season originally premiered in the United Kingdom, on October 18, 2004, on [[Sky1]]. The first season was co-commissioned by Sky Television and Sci-Fi Channel.<ref>{{cite web|last=Otterson|first=Joe|title=NBCUniversal Unveils Originals Slate, Name For Streaming Service|url=https://variety.com/2019/tv/news/battlestar-galactica-reboot-saved-by-the-bell-revival-peacock-nbcuniversal-streaming-service-1203337621/|date=September 17, 2019|website=Variety|access-date=October 30, 2020|archive-date=October 29, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201029072701/https://variety.com/2019/tv/news/battlestar-galactica-reboot-saved-by-the-bell-revival-peacock-nbcuniversal-streaming-service-1203337621/|url-status=live}}</ref> Season 1 began airing in North America three months later, on January 14, 2005, in the United States, and January 15 in Canada. The first episode aired in the U.S. became one of the highest-rated programs ever on [[Syfy|Sci-Fi]], with 3.1 million viewers.<ref>{{cite press release |url=http://www.thefutoncritic.com/ratings/2005/01/19/viewers-embrace-sci-fis-galactica-17669/20050119scifi01/ |title=Viewers Embrace Sci Fi's 'Galactica' |publisher=Sci Fi Channel |date=January 19, 2005 |access-date=June 15, 2011}}</ref> Subsequent episodes proved equally successful.<ref>{{cite press release |url=http://www.thefutoncritic.com/news/2005/04/05/battlestar-galactica-ends-its-first-season-at-number-1-18139/20050405scifi01/ |title=Battlestar Galactica' Ends Its First Season at #1 |publisher=Sci Fi Channel |date=April 5, 2005 |access-date=June 16, 2011}}</ref> The first episode of the season was later made available for viewing in its entirety, and without charge from the Sci-Fi website.<ref name="podcast">{{cite press release |url=http://www.thefutoncritic.com/news/2005/03/09/sci-fi-offers-exclusive-podcast-17965/20050309scifi01/ |title=Sci Fi Offers Exclusive 'Podcast' |publisher=Sci Fi Channel |date=March 9, 2005 |access-date=June 15, 2011}}</ref> Moore also sought to address the "Internet Generation" by posting [[podcast]] commentaries on individual episodes on the official Sci-Fi website.<ref name="podcast"/>

Following the success of the 13-episode first season, the Sci-Fi Channel ordered a 20-episode second season on February 23, 2005.<ref>{{cite press release |url=http://www.thefutoncritic.com/news/2005/02/23/sci-fi-renews-battlestar-galactica-for-second-season-17883/20050223scifi01/ |title=Sci Fi Renews 'Battlestar Galactica' for Second Season |publisher=Sci-Fi Channel |date=February 23, 2005 |access-date=June 30, 2011 }}</ref> The season premiered in the United States on the Sci-Fi Channel on July 15, 2005, with the UK, Ireland, and Canadian premiere in January 2006. In fall 2005, airing of the second season halted, as it was part of Sci-Fi Channel's standard airing schedule normally used for its ''Stargate'' series, which was to split a 20-episode season into two parts (a "winter season" and a "summer season") to avoid heavy competition with major networks that follow a spring/fall schedule. The second half of season 2 ("Season 2.5") began airing on January 6, 2006, after a three-month hiatus.

The Sci-Fi Channel ordered a 20-episode third season on November 16, 2005,<ref>{{cite press release |url=http://www.thefutoncritic.com/news/2005/11/16/sci-fi-channel-charts-a-course-for-battlestar-galactica-season-3-19833/20051116scifi01/ |title=Sci Fi Channel Charts a Course for 'Battlestar Galactica' Season 3 |publisher=Sci-Fi Channel |date=November 16, 2005 |access-date=July 2, 2011 }}</ref> with production beginning in April 2006 in [[Vancouver|Vancouver, British Columbia]].<ref>{{cite press release |url=http://www.thefutoncritic.com/news/2006/03/08/battlestar-galactica-returns-this-fall-20769/20060308scifi01/ |title='Battlestar Galactica' Returns This Fall |publisher=Sci-Fi Channel |date=March 8, 2006 |access-date=July 2, 2011 }}</ref> The season premiered in the United States on October 6, 2006, in Canada the following day, and in the UK on January 9, 2007; with the first two episodes being shown together. The broadcast schedule for season 3 did not include a long hiatus in the middle of the season, as with season 2. The Sci-Fi Channel moved the series to Sundays on January 21, 2007, the first time the show had changed nights since it began airing.<ref>{{cite news |access-date=December 3, 2021 |url=https://variety.com/2006/scene/markets-festivals/new-battlestar-orbit-1117954313/ |title=New 'Battlestar' orbit |work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] |date=November 20, 2006 |last=Martin |first=Denise |archive-date=November 8, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121108145031/http://www.variety.com/article/VR1117954313?refCatId=14 |url-status=live }}</ref> Season 3 was broadcast in [[high-definition television|high-definition]] on [[Sky 1 HD]] in the UK and Ireland, starting on January 9, 2007, and in the U.S. on [[Universal HD]], starting on January 27, 2007.

The Sci-Fi Channel confirmed on May 31, 2007, that ''Battlestar Galactica'' had been renewed for a fourth season of 22 episodes, which producers David Eick and Ronald D. Moore later announced to be the series' last.<ref name="Variety-lastseason">{{cite news |url=https://variety.com/2007/scene/markets-festivals/battlestar-burns-out-next-year-1117966089/ |title='Battlestar' burns out next year |work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] |access-date=January 29, 2022 |date=May 31, 2007 |first=Josef |last=Adalian}}</ref><ref name="LATimes-lastseason">{{cite news |url=http://latimesblogs.latimes.com/showtracker/2007/05/say_it_aint_fra.html |title='Battlestar Galactica': Say it ain't frakkin so! |work=Los Angeles Times |access-date=June 1, 2007 |date=May 31, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070602161919/http://latimesblogs.latimes.com/showtracker/2007/05/say_it_aint_fra.html |archive-date=June 2, 2007 |url-status=live}}</ref> Preceding this was the airing of the ''[[Battlestar Galactica: Razor|Razor]]'' TV movie (comprising two of the ordered broadcast hours), while the remaining season of 20 episodes was split into two halves, due to the [[2007–2008 Writers Guild of America strike]]. The first half comprised episodes 3 to 10, while the second half comprised episodes 11 to 22. The series finale aired on March 20, 2009.

The first two slots of season 4's 22-episode order were taken up by the two-hour TV movie ''Razor'', which was broadcast as an unbroken extended episode detailing the chronicles of the Battlestar ''Pegasus''. It premiered November 24, 2007 in the U.S. and December 18, 2007, in the UK, with a limited U.S. theatrical engagement in major cities, and an extended version was released on DVD the following week.<ref>{{cite web |access-date=May 20, 2008 |url=http://www.tvweek.com/news/2007/03/sci_fi_extends_battlestar.php |title=Sci Fi Extends 'Battlestar Galactica' Fourth Season |work=[[TV Week]] |date=March 21, 2007 |author=Hibberd, James |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080417025213/http://www.tvweek.com/news/2007/03/sci_fi_extends_battlestar.php |archive-date=April 17, 2008 |url-status=live}}</ref> ''Razor'' had [[Michelle Forbes]] reprise her role as Helena Cain, and co-starred Australian actress [[Stephanie Chaves-Jacobsen]], who played [[Kendra Shaw]].

The first half of season 4 (dubbed "Season 4.0" in its DVD release) consisted of ten episodes, and premiered April 4, 2008. The Canadian cable channel [[Space (Canadian TV channel)|Space]] aired season 4 on the same dates. In the UK, Sky1 began airing season 4 on April 15, showing the first two episodes on that date, placing the UK four days behind the U.S. airing. The first part of season 4 began broadcast on [[Universal HD]] on August 30, 2008. In Australia, the first half of season 4 began screening on [[Ten HD]] on September 4, 2008, beginning with ''Razor''. Linking both halves of season 4 together was a set of ten webisodes, which played a similar role to that which ''[[Battlestar Galactica: The Resistance|The Resistance]]'' played between seasons 2 and 3. ''[[Battlestar Galactica: The Face of the Enemy]]'' was released during the weeks leading up to the premiere of episode 13, starting on December 12, 2008, and ending on January 12, 2009.<ref>{{cite web |access-date=November 29, 2008 |url=http://legacy.aintitcool.com/node/39127 |title=Next month's webisodes to reveal shocking Battlestar Galactica secrets |publisher=Ain't It Cool News |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081206034012/http://www.aintitcool.com/node/39127 |archive-date=December 6, 2008 |url-status=live}}</ref> The second half of season 4 (dubbed "Season 4.5", and marketed in the UK as "the Final Season"<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.amazon.co.uk/d/Battlestar-Galactica/Battlestar-Galactica-Final-Season-Part-Two-DVD/B001Q3KA64 |title=Battlestar Galactica - The Final Season (Season 4, Part Two) [DVD] [2009] |publisher=Amazon.co.uk |access-date=April 30, 2017 |archive-date=November 14, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201114001431/https://www.amazon.co.uk/d/Battlestar-Galactica/Battlestar-Galactica-Final-Season-Part-Two-DVD/B001Q3KA64 |url-status=live }}</ref>) consisted of ten episodes, and began airing on January 16, 2009.<ref>{{cite web |access-date=December 3, 2021 |url=https://ew.com/article/2008/10/15/ask-ausiello-1-8/ |title=Ask Ausiello: Spoilers on 'Grey's Anatomy,' 'Prison Break,' 'Bones,' 'Battlestar Galactica,' 'One Tree Hill,' 'Housewives,' and More! |publisher=Entertainment Weekly |archive-date=March 24, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120324124346/http://insidetv.ew.com/2008/10/15/ask-ausiello-1-8/ |url-status=live }}</ref> The season (and series) finale was split into two episodes in the U.S., with the normal-length first part airing on March 13, and the second, with a runtime (including advertisements) of two hours and eleven minutes, airing March 20.<ref>{{cite news |date=March 19, 2009 |access-date=December 3, 2021 |url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/embattlestar-galacticaem_b_176983 |title=Battlestar Galactica Finale DVR Alert! |publisher=HuffPost |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090323082121/http://www.huffingtonpost.com/michael-giltz/embattlestar-galacticaem_b_176983.html |archive-date=March 23, 2009 |url-status=live |first=Michael |last=Giltz}}</ref>

In Australia, the second half of season 4 premiered on the Australian [[Sci Fi Channel (Australia)|Sci-Fi Channel]] on Foxtel January 31, and continued on a weekly basis with each of the remaining episodes of the series airing about six hours after the U.S. broadcast, until the final episode on March 21.<ref>{{cite web |access-date=January 24, 2009 |url=http://www.scifitv.com.au/Blog/2009/01/Bsg-Season-4-Fast-Tracked-By-Satellite-Exclusive-To-Sci-Fi-Australia/ |title=Battlestar Galactica Season 4 Exclusive to Sci Fi! |publisher=scifitv.com.au |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090212164034/http://www.scifitv.com.au/Blog/2009/01/Bsg-Season-4-Fast-Tracked-By-Satellite-Exclusive-To-Sci-Fi-Australia/ |archive-date=February 12, 2009 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

The show re-ran on [[BBC America]] in 2011, including all 4 seasons and the two-part miniseries.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ng |first=Philiana |date=2011-04-21 |title=BBC America Acquires 'Battlestar Galactica' |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/tv/tv-news/bbc-america-acquires-battlestar-galactica-181153/ |access-date=2023-12-14 |website=The Hollywood Reporter |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Continuation ===
On April 27, 2006, the Sci Fi Channel announced that a [[prequel]] [[Spin-off (media)|spin-off]] of ''BSG'' was in development.<ref>{{cite web |access-date=May 20, 2008 |url=http://www.scifi.com/scifiwire/index.php?category=2&id=35773 |title=SCI FI Announces Caprica |publisher=Sci Fi Channel|date=April 27, 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080410172731/http://www.scifi.com/scifiwire/index.php?category=2&id=35773 |archive-date=April 10, 2008 |url-status=dead }}</ref> ''[[Caprica]]'' takes place more than 50 years before the main series, before the original [[Cylon War]], and chronicles the [[Adama Family|Adama family]] and Caprican society, showing the advancement of technology leading to the Cylon revolt.  On March 18, 2008, [[Ronald D. Moore|Ronald Moore]], the head writer, confirmed that ''Caprica'' would in fact be produced beginning with a two-hour [[backdoor pilot]]. On December 2, 2008, SCI FI announced that it had approved the full series. ===Home media===
The miniseries was released in  region 2 on March 1, 2004, and in region 1 on December 28, 2004, and included deleted scenes, audio commentary, and a behind-the-scenes documentary. The first season was released to DVD on March 28, 2005, and September 20, 2005, in region 2 and region 1 respectively and included deleted scenes. The region 1 set also included featurettes, and a tongue-in-cheek promotional special filmed for the Sci Fi Channel in addition to the miniseries.  However, it does not contain the special features that were included on the miniseries stand alone DVD release.

The second season was released in its entirety in a single volume in regions 2 and 4, but issued in two separate volumes (dubbed "Season 2.0" and "Season 2.5") in the region 1, which corresponded with the mid-season break in the broadcast schedule. Each region 1 volume contains half of the season, along with deleted scenes and podcasts that were previously available on the official website. "Season 2.5" also contains an extended version of "Pegasus", the last episode of the first half of the season. The region 2 DVDs include the extended version of "Pegasus", as well as the commentaries and deleted scenes from the region 1 "2.0" release, but do not contain any of the commentaries and deleted scenes from the "2.5" release (other than the extended "Pegasus" episode), nor the original, shorter version of "Pegasus" included on the region 1 "2.0" release. The Canadian DVD release of "Season 2.0" was delayed until April 25, 2006, as the episodes had only begun airing in January 2006.

The third season was released in region 1 on March 18, 2008, in region 2 on September 3, 2007, and in region 4 on November 20, 2007. The region 2 and 4 DVDs do not contain any extras but region 2's box set comes with a 45-minute recap of the previous two seasons (consisting of clips of the seasons strung together with a voice-over). The fourth season, like season 2, was released in two parts. In regions 1, 2 and 4, the television movie ''[[Battlestar Galactica: Razor|Razor]]'' is included in "Season 4.0" (as it is technically a part of the season despite it being released separately at an earlier date). In region 1, however, both the extended and shortened versions of ''Razor'' are included in the "4.0" box set.

On August 14, 2007, Universal Studios Home Entertainment announced that the miniseries and season 1 would be released on December 4, 2007, in region 1, on the now discontinued high definition disc format [[HD DVD]].<ref name="hddvd">{{cite web |title='Battlestar Galactica' Blasts Off on HD DVD |publisher=High-Def Digest |date=August 14, 2007 |url=https://www.highdefdigest.com/news/show/Universal/TV_on_High-Def/Disc_Announcements/Battlestar_Galactica_Blasts_Off_on_HD_DVD/859 |access-date=December 3, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070927230213/http://www.highdefdigest.com/news/show/Universal/TV_on_HighDef/Disc_Announcements/Battlestar_Galactica_Blasts_Off_on_HD_DVD/859 |archive-date=September 27, 2007 |url-status=live}}</ref> The technical specifications include [[1080p]]/[[VC-1]] transfers of the miniseries and each episode is in [[Aspect ratio (image)#16:9|16:9]] [[widescreen]] aspect ratio, plus [[Dolby TrueHD]] [[Surround sound|5.1 surround sound]] and [[Dolby Digital Plus|Dolby Digital-Plus]] 5.1 surround audio options.<ref name="hddvd"/> Each individual season has also subsequently been released on [[Blu-ray Disc]].

The complete series set was released on DVD and Blu-ray Disc on July 28, 2009, in limited edition packaging and with a Cylon Centurion figurine in certain territories. It was re-released on April 6, 2010, in new packaging, with the Region 1 re-release now including ''[[Battlestar Galactica: The Plan|The Plan]]'' TV movie (this was not included in the Region 2 release).<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.tvshowsondvd.com/shows/Battlestar-Galactica/8735 |title=Battlestar Galactica (2004) |publisher=TVShowsOnDVD |access-date=August 21, 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100405113725/http://www.tvshowsondvd.com/shows/Battlestar-Galactica/8735 |archive-date=April 5, 2010 }}</ref>

== Reception ==

=== Critical response ===

==== Praise ====
Throughout its run, the series earned critical acclaim from ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'', ''[[National Review]]'', ''[[Rolling Stone]]'',<ref name="intergalactic_terror"/> ''[[Newsday]]'', ''[[The New York Times]]'', ''[[The New Yorker]]'', the ''[[San Francisco Chronicle]]'', the ''[[Chicago Tribune]]'', and ''[[Entertainment Weekly]]''.<ref name=ews2>{{cite magazine |author=Fonseca, Nicholas |url=https://ew.com/article/2006/06/12/dear-emmy-voters/ |title=Honors Class |date=June 14, 2006 |magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]] |access-date=January 18, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090209040916/http://www.ew.com/ew/article/0%2C%2C1202270_2%2C00.html |archive-date=February 9, 2009 |url-status=live }}</ref>

Diane Werts of ''Newsday'' wrote: "You can look at this saga any way you want—as political drama, religious debate, psychological suspenser, sci-fi adventure, deep metaphor or just plain fun—and it's scintillating from every angle."<ref name=newsday051225>{{cite news |last=Werts |first= Diane |url=http://www.newsday.com/news/columnists/ny-fftv4561321dec25,0,4040253.story |title=The Best of 2005 Television |date=December 25, 2005 |work=[[Newsday]] |access-date=January 18, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090618002509/http://www.newsday.com/news/columnists/ny-fftv4561321dec25%2C0%2C4040253.story |archive-date=June 18, 2009 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Robert Bianco of ''[[USA Today]]'' commented: "Driven by violence and rage, ''Galactica'' is perhaps the darkest space opera American TV has ever produced. In ''Galactica''{{'s}} future, humans are on the run, and if external enemies don't get us, internal divisions will... You'll understand them [the characters], their conflicts and their desires, because they're recognizable humans in all their glorious complexity. And that's what makes ''Galactica'' a great TV series."<ref name=usatoday050714>{{cite news |last=Bianco |first=Robert |url=https://usatoday30.usatoday.com/life/television/news/2005-07-14-battlestar_x.htm |title='Galactica' back, better than ever |date=July 14, 2005 |work=[[USA Today]] |access-date=December 3, 2009 |archive-date=April 27, 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060427220357/http://www.usatoday.com/life/television/news/2005-07-14-battlestar_x.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> Peter Suderman of ''National Review'' stated that the series is "arguably the most potent, dramatically vibrant series on television. ...[I]t packs the power of a gut punch on screen. For that, much credit is due to the immensely compelling cast of characters... ''Battlestar Galactica'' burns with a combustive mixture of political turmoil and human drama that is as achingly real and relevant as anything on television.<ref name=nr060120>{{cite news |last=Suderman |first= Peter |url=https://www.nationalreview.com/2006/01/starborn-society-peter-suderman/ |title=Starborn Society |date=January 20, 2006 |work=[[National Review]] |access-date=December 3, 2021  |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120118142406/http://old.nationalreview.com/comment/suderman200601200838.asp |archive-date=January 18, 2012 |df=mdy}}</ref> Jeff Jensen of ''Entertainment Weekly'' wrote that the show "has distinguished itself as one of television's very best dramas — on a par with ''[[24 (TV series)|24]]'', ''[[The Wire]]'', and ''[[Lost (2004 TV series)|Lost]]'' — because it so utterly transcends both its genre and its source material. ...[The] series' sophisticated stories have also attracted a distinctively new breed of fan, one who's not necessarily a sci-fi buff."<ref name=ew060921>{{cite magazine |last=Jensen |first=Jeff |url=https://ew.com/article/2006/09/22/battlestar-galactica-inside-tvs-next-great-cult-hit/ |title=Great Space Coasters |date=September 21, 2006 |magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]] |access-date=February 17, 2009 |archive-date=January 2, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090102060539/http://www.ew.com/ew/article/0,,1537626,00.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Moreover, in 2012, ''Entertainment Weekly'' listed the show at #7 in the "25 Best Cult TV Shows from the Past 25 Years," saying that producer Moore "expanded the show's central premise into an addictive post-[[September 11 attacks|9/11]] parable and one of the most critically acclaimed series of the decade." The article credited Starbuck and Number Six as "geek and feminist icons," adding, "best of all, the show introduced this peerless profanity into the national lexicon: ''Frak''{{thinsp}}!"<ref>"25 Best Cult TV Shows from the Past 25 Years." ''[[Entertainment Weekly]]''. August 3, 2012, p. 40.</ref>

Mary McNamara of the ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' praised the show's ability to "anchor fantasy with vivid and recognizable human psychology" and declares that the series is "not just a cult hit but a significant piece of television."<ref name=lat090116>{{cite news |last=McNamara |first=Mary |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2009-jan-16-et-battlestar-galactica16-story.html |title='Battlestar' crew confronts a terrible reality |date=January 16, 2009 |work=Los Angeles Times |access-date=January 16, 2009 |archive-date=January 11, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120111165549/http://articles.latimes.com/2009/jan/16/entertainment/et-battlestar-galactica16 |url-status=live }}</ref> Maureen Ryan of the ''Chicago Tribune'' described it as a "sprawling, enthralling tale of human survival"<ref name=ct070702>{{cite news |last=Ryan |first= Maureen |url=http://featuresblogs.chicagotribune.com/entertainment_tv/best_and_worst_of_2007_tv/ |title=Simon Cowell, Isaiah Washington and Tila Tequila: Revisiting 2007's low points|date=July 2, 2007 |work=[[Chicago Tribune]] |access-date=January 18, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081218210859/http://featuresblogs.chicagotribune.com/entertainment_tv/best_and_worst_of_2007_tv/ |archive-date=December 18, 2008 |url-status=dead}}</ref> that is "full of political allegories and fascinating, multifaceted characters."<ref name=ct081217>{{cite news |last=Ryan |first= Maureen |url=http://featuresblogs.chicagotribune.com/entertainment_tv/best_and_worst_of_2008_tv/ |title=The Top TV shows of 2008 |date=December 17, 2008 |work=[[Chicago Tribune]] |access-date=January 18, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081219222938/http://featuresblogs.chicagotribune.com/entertainment_tv/best_and_worst_of_2008_tv/ |archive-date=December 19, 2008 |url-status=live}}</ref> She finds, "Like ''[[Deadwood (TV series)|Deadwood]]'', ''Battlestar Galactica'' is interested in exploring how a society on the edge decides to govern itself. What rights and actions are sacrosanct, which are outlawed, when most of the human race is eliminated? ... Thanks to a stellar cast and brave writing, ''Battlestar'' soars."<ref name=ct061214>{{cite news |last=Ryan |first= Maureen |url=http://featuresblogs.chicagotribune.com/entertainment_tv/2006/12/the_top_10_show.html |title=The Top 10 shows of 2006 (and 10 runners up) |date=December 14, 2006 |work=[[Chicago Tribune]] |access-date=January 18, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090208133618/http://featuresblogs.chicagotribune.com/entertainment_tv/2006/12/the_top_10_show.html |archive-date=February 8, 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref> Throughout its run, the series has often surprised reviewers with its many twists and turns. Ryan comments: "There's nothing like a good ''Battlestar'' [[plot twist]] to make your head spin, but the 'holy cow' moments aren't the main point (though they're one heck of a tasty side dish). The show and its twists and turns are grounded in deep curiosity about human nature, and how contradictory and confounding it can be."<ref name=ct071214>{{cite news |last= Ryan |first= Maureen |url=http://featuresblogs.chicagotribune.com/entertainment_tv/2007/12/year-end-extrav.html |title=Year-end extravaganza: My Top 10 TV shows (and the runners up) |date=December 14, 2007 |work=[[Chicago Tribune]] |access-date=January 18, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090114093204/http://featuresblogs.chicagotribune.com/entertainment_tv/2007/12/year-end-extrav.html |archive-date=January 14, 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref>

Matt Soergel of ''[[The Florida Times-Union]]'' stated: "Its propulsive and complex storytelling is matched by, at best, just a handful of theatrical movies a year."<ref name=ftu090115>{{cite news |author=Soergel, Matt |url=http://jaxairnews.jacksonville.com/entertainment/tv/2009-01-13/story/still_time_to_get_onboard_brilliant_sci_fi_series |title=Still time to get onboard brilliant sci-fi series |date=January 15, 2009 |work=[[The Florida Times-Union]] |access-date=January 16, 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120429182934/http://jaxairnews.jacksonville.com/entertainment/tv/2009-01-13/story/still_time_to_get_onboard_brilliant_sci_fi_series |archive-date=April 29, 2012 }}</ref> Tim Goodman of the ''San Francisco Chronicle'' opines, "''Battlestar Galactica'' transcends the sci-fi genre; it competes, creatively, on the same level as any other top-tier drama."<ref name=sfc090114>{{cite news |last=Goodman |first= Tim |url=https://www.sfgate.com/news/article/BSG-FNL-return-3254550.php |title='BSG,' 'FNL' return |date=January 14, 2009 |work=[[The San Francisco Chronicle]] |access-date=January 15, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090209000048/https://www.sfgate.com/news/article/BSG-FNL-return-3254550.php |archive-date=February 9, 2009 |url-status=live }}</ref> Mark Perigard of the ''[[Boston Herald]]'' stated: "A drama this gripping comes 'round rarely."<ref name=bh090116>{{cite news |author=Perigard, Mark. A. |url=https://www.bostonherald.com/2009/01/16/battlestar-galactica-delivers/ |title='Battlestar Galactica' delivers |date=January 16, 2009 |work=[[Boston Herald]] |access-date=December 3, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090121130904/http://bostonherald.com/entertainment/television/reviews/view.bg?articleid=1145538 |archive-date=January 21, 2009 |url-status=live}}</ref> James Poniewozik of ''[[Time (magazine)|Time]]'' magazine named it one of the 100 best TV shows of all time.<ref name=top100 /> ''Time'' also wrote in the spring of 2005 that the new show was one of the six best drama programs on television. The series has also received favorable reviews from other writers. Joss Whedon |url=http://www.wizarduniverse.com/magazine/wizard/000495675.cfm?page=3 |website=[[Wizard Entertainment]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061111115705/http://www.wizarduniverse.com/magazine/wizard/000495675.cfm?page=3 |archive-date=November 11, 2006 |page=3 |url-status=dead |quote=But I just watched the miniseries opener of "Battlestar Galactica" and I loved the toes off that bitch. I’m not positive what that phrase means. But tension, drama, humanity, and—alien spaceships. I was pretty floored. That’s my call. }}</ref>

On [[review aggregator]] website [[Rotten Tomatoes]], the first season has an approval rating of 90% with an average score of 8.4/10 based on 20 reviews; with a critics consensus stating, "A captivating combination of riveting political drama and science fiction fantasy make ''Battlestar Galactica'' must-see sci-fi."<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/tv/battlestar-galactica/s01 |title=Battlestar Galactica: Season 1 |website=Rotten Tomatoes |access-date=April 26, 2024}}</ref> The second season has an approval rating of 100% with an average score of 9.5/10 based on 12 reviews; with a critics consensus stating, "In its second season, ''Battlestar Galatica'' doubles down on the series' high-minded themes and satisfyingly complex storylines."<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/tv/battlestar-galactica/s02 |title=Battlestar Galactica: Season 2 |website=Rotten Tomatoes |access-date=April 26, 2024}}</ref> The third season has an approval rating of 100% with an average score of 9/10 based on 20 reviews; with a critics consensus stating, "Dark, charming and unusually thoughtful, ''Battlestar Galactica''{{'}}s third season continues to improve on the show's most addictive elements."<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/tv/battlestar-galactica/s03 |title=Battlestar Galactica: Season 3 |website=Rotten Tomatoes |access-date=April 26, 2024}}</ref> The fourth season has an approval rating of 92% with an average score of 8.1/10 based on 38 reviews; with a critics consensus stating, "''Battlestar Galactica''{{'}}s final season proves a satisfying conclusion to TV's best science fiction offering."<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rottentomatoes.com/tv/battlestar-galactica/s04 |title=Battlestar Galactica: Season 4 |website=Rotten Tomatoes |access-date=April 26, 2024}}</ref> On [[Metacritic]], seasons 1 and 2 have a score of 89/100, season 3 is scored 94/100, and season 4 is scored 85/100.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.metacritic.com/tv/battlestar-galactica-2003/ |title=Battlestar Galactica (2003) |website=Metacritic |access-date=April 26, 2024}}</ref>

==== Criticism ====
Some fans of the original 1970s series opposed the new series since the time it premiered, due to what was perceived as its darker, more confused tone.  In a May 2004 article from ''[[Dreamwatch]]'' magazine titled "Starbuck: Lost in Castration", [[Dirk Benedict]], who portrayed [[Lieutenant Starbuck]] in the original series, harshly criticized the new series, citing its dark tone and supposed moral relativism.<ref name=":0">{{cite web |url=http://www.dirkbenedictcentral.com/home/articles-readarticle.php?nid=5 |title=Starbuck: Lost in Castration |work=Dreamwatch |date=May 2004 |access-date=August 2, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131220100737/http://www.dirkbenedictcentral.com/home/articles-readarticle.php?nid=5 |archive-date=December 20, 2013 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Benedict devoted the greatest part of the article to criticizing the producers' decision to turn Starbuck into a female character, tying it in to what he perceived as a general anti-masculinity agenda.<ref name=":0" />

Other critics, even those who wrote rave reviews about the first two seasons of the series, felt that a major drop in quality occurred in the third season, continuing into the fourth and final season.  In particular, the controversial series finale drew heavy criticism, largely due to the view that it failed to explain many of the main plotlines which had been teased throughout the series' run.  Charlie Jane Anders of io9.com wrote:

{{blockquote|Even ''Battlestar Galactica'' couldn't be ''Battlestar Galactica'' for longer than a few years. By halfway through the third season, the cracks are pretty apparent, as the show detours into romance subplots. The writers start throwing out curveballs like randomly selected Cylons and Starbuck's inexplicable (and unexplained) resurrection. By the time the show ended, its mystique was somewhat tarnished, and its ending remains controversial.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://gizmodo.com/why-doesnt-syfy-have-a-show-like-battlestar-galactica-a-5959935 |title=Why doesn't Syfy have a show like ''Battlestar Galactica'' any more? |publisher=Gizmodo|first=Charlie Jane |last=Anders |date=April 19, 2013 |access-date=December 3, 2021 |archive-date=March 31, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130331000905/http://io9.com/5959935/why-doesnt-syfy-have-a-show-like-battlestar-galactica-any-more |url-status=live }}</ref>}}

Anders later included the series on her list of "10 Once-Great TV Shows (And The Exact Moments They Started to Suck)", saying:

{{blockquote|There was a time, not long ago, when BSG was considered the gold standard for science fiction television. Tense, multilayered, complicated, and filled with morally gray characters — it was all the things we always clamor for but seldom get. The show stumbled somewhat in its third season, with the boxing episode and a boring love triangle. But it didn't actually become raw suckage until Starbuck died for no reason, and then came back from the dead for no reason. The writers have basically admitted they had no plan for killing and resurrecting Starbuck — they just thought it would be a cool thing to do, and they would figure out the reasons later. And thus, we ended up with a year of Starbuck Interrupted, constantly shouting "You're going the wrong way!" and playing the piano while talking about her daddy.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://gizmodo.com/10-once-great-tv-shows-and-the-exact-moment-they-start-476467737 |title=10 Once-Great TV Shows (And The Exact Moments They Started to Suck) |publisher=Gizmodo |first=Charlie Jane |last=Anders |date=November 12, 2012 |access-date=December 3, 2021 |archive-date=August 15, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130815025021/http://io9.com/10-once-great-tv-shows-and-the-exact-moment-they-start-476467737 |url-status=live }}</ref>}}

In a ''[[Commentary (magazine)|Commentary]]'' article on the prevalence of [[Bush Derangement Syndrome]] in popular culture, conservative political commentator [[Jonah Goldberg]] analyzed the show's "radically bizarre and nonsensical turn of events ... that led inexorably to its self-destruction":

{{blockquote|Originally, the series was very difficult to pigeonhole ideologically. ... When it came time to make the third season ... a show marked by gritty realism about how a decent but flawed civilization modeled on our own tries to cling to its decency while fighting an existential war against an implacable enemy veered wildly off course. The humans were no longer analogized to Americans; rather Americans were analogized to [[genocidal]] occupiers. In other words, we are no longer the inspiration for the futuristic Israelites trying to survive. We are now the [[Nazis]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.commentarymagazine.com/article/how-politics-destroyed-a-great-tv-show/ |title=How Politics Destroyed a Great TV Show |magazine=[[Commentary (magazine)|Commentary]] |first=Jonah |last=Goldberg |date=October 1, 2009 |access-date=June 15, 2015 |archive-date=April 28, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140428125333/http://www.commentarymagazine.com/article/how-politics-destroyed-a-great-tv-show/ |url-status=live }}</ref>}}

Fantasy author [[George R.R. Martin]] expressed his dissatisfaction with how the writers handled the ending of the TV series, commenting:

{{blockquote|''Battlestar Galactica'' ends with 'God Did It.' Looks like somebody skipped Writing 101, when you learn that a deus ex machina is a crappy way to end a story... Yeah, yeah, sometimes the journey is its own reward. I certainly enjoyed much of the journey with BSG... But damn it, doesn't anybody know how to write an ending any more?  Writing 101, kids. Adam and Eve, God Did It, It Was All a Dream? I've seen [[Clarion West Writers Workshop|Clarion]] students left stunned and bleeding for turning in stories with those endings.<ref>{{cite web |last=Martin |first=George R.R. |title=Writing 101 |publisher=Not A Blog |date=April 5, 2009 |url=http://grrm.livejournal.com/82239.html |access-date=July 30, 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140422022724/http://grrm.livejournal.com/82239.html |archive-date=April 22, 2014 |df=mdy-all}}</ref>}}

Josh Tyler of ''[[CinemaBlend]]'' concluded that the series finale made no real attempt to resolve any of the plotlines or mysteries set up during the earlier run of the show.<ref>{{cite web |last=Tyler |first=Josh |title=Why The Battlestar Galactica Finale Is A Huge Cop Out And It Doesn't Matter |work=CinemaBlend |date=March 20, 2009 |url=https://cinemablend.com/television/Why-The-Battlestar-Galactica-Finale-Is-A-Huge-Copout-And-It-Doesn-t-Matter-16337.html |access-date=October 17, 2011 |archive-date=November 24, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111124212710/http://www.cinemablend.com/television/Why-The-Battlestar-Galactica-Finale-Is-A-Huge-Copout-And-It-Doesn-t-Matter-16337.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Wider influence ===
On March 17, 2009, the [[United Nations]] hosted a ''Battlestar Galactica'' retrospective including a discussion with [[Mary McDonnell]], [[Edward James Olmos]], [[Ronald D. Moore]] and [[David Eick]] on [[human rights]], [[terrorism]], children and [[War|armed conflict]], and reconciliation between civilians and faiths. The discussion was moderated by actress [[Whoopi Goldberg]] and also included [[Radhika Coomaraswamy]], the [[Diplomatic rank|Special Representative]] of the Secretary-General for Children and Armed Conflict; [[Craig Mokhiber]] of the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights; [[Robert C. Orr]], Assistant Secretary-General for Policy Planning; and Famatta Rose Osode, from the Permanent Mission of Liberia to the UN.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.un.org/apps/news/story.asp?NewsID=30217&Cr=television&Cr1= |title=UN and Battlestar Galactica host discussion of human rights and armed conflict |publisher=UN News Centre |date=March 17, 2009 |access-date=August 21, 2011 |archive-date=January 15, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120115041341/http://www.un.org/apps/news/story.asp?NewsID=30217&Cr=television&Cr1= |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |url=http://popwatch.ew.com/2009/03/18/galactica-un/ |title='Battlestar Galactica' at the UN: A night of geekery, human rights, and fantastic curtains |magazine=Entertainment Weekly |last=Bernardin |first=Marc |date=March 18, 2009 |access-date=August 21, 2011 |archive-date=October 5, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111005233250/http://popwatch.ew.com/2009/03/18/galactica-un/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

''Battlestar Galactica'' was the basis for a special session at the 2009 [[World Science Festival]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://worldsciencefestival.com/events/battlestar_galactica_cyborgs_on_the_horizon |title=Battlestar Galactica Cyborgs on the Horizon |publisher=World Science Festival |access-date=August 21, 2011 |archive-date=August 26, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110826081112/http://worldsciencefestival.com/events/battlestar_galactica_cyborgs_on_the_horizon |url-status=live }}</ref> The session included presentations from [[Mary McDonnell]] and [[Michael Hogan (Canadian actor)|Michael Hogan]], as well as scientists [[Hod Lipson]] and [[Kevin Warwick]].

The [[Experience Music Project and Science Fiction Museum and Hall of Fame]] in Seattle organised a special exhibition on the series with props of three spacecraft models and guest speakers starting October 23, 2010.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.empmuseum.org/exhibitions/index.asp?articleID=1491 |title=EMPSFM: Battlestar Galactica: The Exhibition |publisher=EMP Museum |access-date=August 21, 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110812112555/http://www.empmuseum.org/exhibitions/index.asp?articleID=1491 |archive-date=August 12, 2011 }}</ref>
